title: Access to pathology and laboratory medicine services: a crucial gap
key_fact_extracted: Lancet PALM Series paper 1. Series press summary: ~1 pathologist per 1,000,000 population in sub-Saharan Africa vs ~1 per 15,000-20,000 in US/UK (ratio ~50x). Full text paywalled: exact in-text wording UNVERIFIED.

title: Improving pathology and laboratory medicine in low-income and middle-income countries: roadmap to solutions
key_fact_extracted: Lancet PALM Series paper 2 (roadmap). Secondary sources attribute to this Series the estimate that at current training rates (~80 pathologists graduate/yr in SSA) it would take ~400 years for SSA to reach the US/UK pathologist:population ratio. UNVERIFIED against full text.

title: Delivering modern, high-quality, affordable pathology and laboratory medicine to low-income and middle-income countries: a call to action
key_fact_extracted: Lancet PALM Series paper 3: call to action on delivering affordable pathology & laboratory medicine to LMICs; argues PALM investment is affordable and essential for UHC. No quantitative figure verified (paywalled).

title: The Lancet Commission on diagnostics: transforming access to diagnostics
key_fact_extracted: 47% of the global population has little or no access to diagnostics; only ~19% of populations in low- and lower-middle-income countries have access to the simplest diagnostic tests at primary care (60-70% in hospitals); diagnostic gap for six tracer conditions 35-62%, the largest gap in the care cascade.

title: Oncologic Care and Pathology Resources in Africa: Survey and Recommendations
key_fact_extracted: Survey of African pathology resources: pathologists per population ranged from 9,264,500 persons per pathologist (Niger) to 84,133 (Mauritius) vs an estimated 15,000-20,000 persons per pathologist in the UK/US; e.g. Tanzania 22 pathologists for 48.1 M; Sierra Leone 1 pathologist for 6.4 M; South Sudan 2 for 12.2 M.

title: Improvement of pathology in sub-Saharan Africa
key_fact_extracted: 2012-13 survey of SSA pathology capacity; cited by later work as showing all SSA countries except Botswana and South Africa have fewer than one pathologist per 500,000 people, several at ~1 per million, Somalia none. Figures taken from secondary citation; UNVERIFIED against full text.

title: Trends in the US and Canadian Pathologist Workforces From 2007 to 2017
key_fact_extracted: US active pathologists fell from 15,568 (2007) to 12,839 (2017), -17.5%; Canada rose from 1,467 to 1,767 (+20.5%). Context: even HICs face pathologist supply pressure.

title: An Essential Pathology Package for Low- and Middle-Income Countries
key_fact_extracted: Essential pathology package: equipment needs ~$2,000-5,000 for a tier-1 primary facility lab vs $150,000-200,000 for a district hospital laboratory; recurrent lab costs ~6% of hospital budget in mid-sized hospitals.

title: Economic savings for scientific free and open source technology: A review
key_fact_extracted: Review of free/open-source scientific hardware: average savings 87% vs proprietary equivalents; 89% with Arduino, 92% with RepRap-class 3-D printing, 94% combining both.

title: Open hardware: From DIY trend to global transformation in access to laboratory equipment
key_fact_extracted: Perspective on open hardware as a route to laboratory-equipment access globally (incl. LMICs); frames 3D-printed open designs as a transformation in access. Qualitative.

title: The mechanics of paraffin sectioning by the microtome
key_fact_extracted: Classic analysis of knife geometry (bevel, clearance/tilt, rake) and the mechanics of paraffin sectioning; foundation for clearance-angle recommendations. Full text not retrieved: specific angle values UNVERIFIED.

title: Distortions due to the sliding microtome
key_fact_extracted: Companion paper: distortions produced by the sliding microtome (section compression and displacement). Details UNVERIFIED.

title: Paraffin Compression Due to the Rotary Microtome
key_fact_extracted: Paraffin compression on the rotary microtome: thick sections commonly compressed 15% or more; for sections below 5-10 um compression may exceed 50%.

title: The Relationship of Microtome Knife Facet Bevels to Edge Effectiveness in Cutting Paraffin Sections
key_fact_extracted: Knives with the usual ~31 deg facet bevel gave gross paraffin compression at 4 um or thinner; a 21 deg facet bevel produced a superior 4 um ribbon with little folding; cell morphology unaffected by the edge change.

title: Monitoring cutting forces with an instrumented histological microtome
key_fact_extracted: Histological microtome knife mount instrumented to sense knife load during the cut; variation in cutting force reports the texture of the sample. Only known instrumented-microtome force measurement found; absolute force values (N) not in abstract - UNVERIFIED.

title: “Cracking” and “chatter” in paraffin sections
journal: The Journal of Pathology and Bacteriology
key_fact_extracted: Early pathology-literature description of 'cracking' and 'chatter' artefacts in paraffin sections (title-level verification only).

title: Knife chatter during thin sectioning of rat incisor enamel can cause periodicities resembling cross‐striations
key_fact_extracted: Knife chatter during thin sectioning produces periodic artefacts (in enamel) that can be mistaken for real structure - demonstrates chatter as a vibration-driven periodic thickness modulation.

title: Minimal compression of ultrathin sections with use of an oscillating diamond knife
key_fact_extracted: Conventional ultrathin sectioning compresses sections by 20-35% of section height (45 deg diamond knife); oscillating the knife laterally minimises compression.

title: Cutting artefacts and cutting process in vitreous sections for cryo-electron microscopy
key_fact_extracted: Analysis of cutting artefacts (compression, crevasses, knife marks) and the cutting process in vitreous cryosections; compression scales with knife/sectioning angle. Specific numbers UNVERIFIED (abstract not available).

title: Cutting, by ‘pressing and slicing,’ of thin floppy slices of materials illustrated by experiments on cheddar cheese and salami
key_fact_extracted: Fracture-mechanics treatment of cutting floppy thin slices by combined pressing and slicing: adding a slicing (tangential) component to the blade motion lowers the normal cutting force (slice-push ratio). Numerical values UNVERIFIED.

authors: Reyssat; Tallinen; Le Merrer et al.
title: Slicing Softly with Shear
key_fact_extracted: Physics of slicing soft solids: blade shear/slicing motion strongly reduces the force needed to initiate and propagate a cut relative to pure pressing.

title: Direct Measurement and AI-based Inference Reveal Histological Section Thickness as a Variable Physical Property Accessible from Routine H&E Images
key_fact_extracted: Direct measurement of paraffin section thickness: >2/3 of 154 measurements fell outside +/-10% of the microtome preset value; CNN inference of thickness achieved R2 0.86, MAE 0.28 um. Shows actual thickness deviates substantially from dial setting even on commercial microtomes.

title: Caldwell’s Automatic Microtome
key_fact_extracted: Caldwell's (Caldwell-Threlfall) automatic microtome, Cambridge 1883-84: hand-worked, delivers a continuous ribbon of accurately cut sections at ~100 sections per minute - the ribbon-cutting precursor of Darwin's rocker.

title: On Two Forms of Automatic Microtomes
key_fact_extracted: Minot describes two forms of automatic (rotary-type) microtomes; the Minot design (specimen moves vertically past a fixed knife with automatic screw feed) became the archetype of the rotary microtome.

title: THE ORIGIN OF THE AUTOMATIC MICROTOME
key_fact_extracted: First-hand account of the origin of the automatic microtome in Cambridge (Caldwell & Threlfall, early 1880s), preceding Horace Darwin's 1885 rocking microtome.

title: The History of Histology: A Brief Survey of Sources
key_fact_extracted: Survey of sources for the history of histology/microtechnique (Bracegirdle's 1978 book 'A History of Microtechnique' is the standard monograph on microtome evolution).

title: Cutting of sections for electron microscopy with a modified “Cambridge” Rocking Microtome
key_fact_extracted: A modified Cambridge rocking microtome was used to cut sections for electron microscopy - evidence that the rocking-arm kinematics are capable of very thin sections when feed and stiffness are adequate.

title: The rapid-tome, a 3D-printed microtome, and an updated hand-sectioning method for high-quality plant sectioning
key_fact_extracted: Rapid-Tome: 3D-printed (approx. 18 h print) plant microtome assembled with five hardware-store metal parts; produces hand-fed sections of fresh/woody stems <100 um; no paraffin capability, no micrometer feed, cost stated only as 'a fraction' of a commercial microtome.

title: Low cost, portable, 3D printable tissue precision slicer
key_fact_extracted: HardwareX tissue precision slicer: ~US$853 BOM, 3D-printed Nylon-12, razor-blade cutting, slice thickness range 250 um - 1 mm (claims 0.25 um stage positioning accuracy); ~1 min per slice; notes basic vibratomes cost US$5,000-15,000 and advanced US$20,000-50,000.

title: An Inexpensive Vibrating Microtome for Sectioning Fixed Tissue
key_fact_extracted: Inexpensive vibrating microtome built from a hair clipper and a nut-and-bolt advance for <US$50 (1980); fixed tissue sections uniform at 50 um or more.

title: CONSTRUCTION OF A PRECISION HAND MICROTOME FROM AN INEXPENSIVE MICROMETER
key_fact_extracted: Precision hand microtome built from a brass tube and a micrometer whose spindle advances the specimen for razor-blade sectioning (botanical use; thickness not quantified in abstract).

title: Robotic microscopy for everyone: the OpenFlexure microscope
key_fact_extracted: OpenFlexure: open-source, 3D-printed, motorised laboratory microscope; >100 units produced locally in Tanzania and Kenya for education, research and clinical use - complementary low-cost imaging side.

title: A one-piece 3D printed flexure translation stage for open-source microscopy
key_fact_extracted: Monolithic 3D-printed (plastic) flexure translation stage achieving sub-micron motion over 8 x 8 x 4 mm with drift <20 um per week without temperature control - evidence that FDM compliant mechanisms can reach micron-scale precision.

title: The Theory of Symmetrical Crossed Flexure Pivots
journal: Australian Journal of Scientific Research Series A: Physical Sciences
key_fact_extracted: Original small-deflection theory of the symmetrical crossed flexure pivot: rotational stiffness of form K = (n E I / L) f(lambda) and second-order (theta^2) centre shift; the crossing point location lambda controls both.

title: The properties of crossed flexure pivots, and the influence of the point at which the strips cross
key_fact_extracted: Shows the influence of the point at which the strips cross: centre shift is minimised (to first order zero) when the strips cross at ~12.73% of their length from the moving end (lambda ~ 0.1273), at the cost of higher stiffness; pivots widely used to replace knife edges and ball bearings.

title: The cross-spring pivot as a constructional element
key_fact_extracted: Large-deflection (elliptic-integral) analysis of the cross-spring pivot as a constructional element; establishes parasitic-shift phase phi = theta/2 and stiffness-vs-load behaviour.

title: An Investigation of the Cross-Spring Pivot
key_fact_extracted: Experimental investigation of the cross-spring pivot; gave rule-of-thumb formulas for spring constant, bending stress and pivot-point motion.

title: Analytical and experimental characterisation of high-precision flexural pivots subjected to lateral loads
key_fact_extracted: Analytical (elliptic-integral) and experimental characterisation of high-precision cross-spring flexural pivots under lateral loads: stiffness and parasitic shift depend on load; experimental validation of the models.

title: The modeling of cross-axis flexural pivots
key_fact_extracted: Pseudo-rigid-body (four-bar) model of cross-axis flexural pivots giving closed-form stiffness and centre-shift estimates validated vs FEA.

title: Stiffness and stress characteristics of the generalized cross-spring pivot
key_fact_extracted: Non-dimensional model of stiffness and stress of the generalized cross-spring pivot (arbitrary crossing point lambda).

title: Accuracy characteristics of the generalized cross-spring pivot
key_fact_extracted: Accuracy model of generalized cross-spring pivot up to +/-15 deg: centre-shift component along the symmetry axis is second order in theta, the transverse component third order; locating the crossing point appropriately minimises shift; notes cartwheel pivots give ~5x smaller centre shift than a standard cross-spring pivot.

title: Optimized cross-spring pivot configurations with minimized parasitic shifts and stiffness variations investigated via nonlinear FEA
journal: Mechanics Based Design of Structures and Machines
key_fact_extracted: Nonlinear FEA: parasitic shift minimised for lambda in 0.127-0.133 (alpha=30 deg) or 0.127-0.1305 (alpha=45 deg); shift phase phi = theta/2; 'butterfly' compound configurations reduce parasitic shift up to 8x.

title: Triple Crossed Flexure Pivot Based on a Zero Parasitic Center Shift Kinematic Design
key_fact_extracted: Flexure pivots have no play or contact friction and can be monolithic, but show a parasitic centre shift proportional to theta^2; TRIVOT geometry nulls it kinematically; classical CFP shift computed from Wittrick's equations normalised by strip length L.

title: 2D shape optimization of leaf-type crossed flexure pivot springs for minimum stress
key_fact_extracted: 2D shape optimisation of leaf-type crossed flexure pivot springs to minimise peak stress (and thereby improve fatigue life) for aerospace actuators.

title: <title>Fatigue failure of thin wire-electrodischarge-machined flexure hinges</title>
key_fact_extracted: Fatigue tests on 66 wire-EDM steel and bronze flexure hinges with 50 um thin sections: admissible stresses for low-roughness (Ra 0.2 um) flexures are at least as high as for standard fatigue specimens - supports using bulk spring-steel S-N data for thin flexure blades.

title: Flexures
key_fact_extracted: Textbook 'Flexures: Elements of Elastic Mechanisms': design equations for leaf-spring, notch, cross-strip and parallelogram flexures incl. stiffness, stress and parasitic motion.

title: Monolithic 2 DOF fully compliant space pointing mechanism
key_fact_extracted: 3D-printed (titanium) monolithic fully compliant 2-DOF pointing mechanism - demonstrates additive manufacturing of compliant mechanisms.

title: Foundations of Ultra-Precision Mechanism Design
key_fact_extracted: Textbook 'Foundations of Ultra-Precision Mechanism Design': differential screw principle - net advance per revolution equals the difference of the two pitches (e.g. 1.25 - 1.00 = 0.25 mm/rev), with discussion of friction/backlash in fine-adjustment screws and flexure guides.

title: Mechanical properties of components fabricated with open-source 3-D printers under realistic environmental conditions
key_fact_extracted: FDM parts from open-source RepRap printers: average tensile strength 56.6 MPa (PLA) and 28.5 MPa (ABS); average elastic modulus 3368 MPa (PLA) and 1807 MPa (ABS).

title: Material Property Testing of 3D-Printed Specimen in PLA on an Entry-Level 3D Printer
key_fact_extracted: Entry-level printer PLA: UTS 64 MPa at 45 deg raster, 58 MPa (0 deg) and 54 MPa (90 deg); flexural strength 102 MPa (0 deg); fatigue tested.

title: Additive manufacturing of PLA structures using fused deposition modelling: Effect of process parameters on mechanical properties and their optimal selection
key_fact_extracted: Effect of build orientation, layer thickness and feed rate on PLA tensile/flexural properties: upright (Z) orientation weakest; recommends parameter selection. Values UNVERIFIED (abstract not retrieved).

title: FDM process parameters influence over the mechanical properties of polymer specimens: A review
key_fact_extracted: Review of FDM process-parameter effects (orientation, raster, layer height, infill, temperature) on mechanical properties of printed polymers.

title: Effect of Printing Parameters on the Thermal and Mechanical Properties of 3D-Printed PLA and PETG, Using Fused Deposition Modeling
key_fact_extracted: PLA and PETG printed parts show pronounced tension/compression asymmetry; tensile, compressive, bending and thermal-deformation properties measured vs print temperature and speed.

title: Experimental investigation of mechanical properties of PLA, ABS, and PETG 3-d printing materials using fused deposition modeling technique
key_fact_extracted: PLA, PETG and ABS printed at several raster angles: PLA at 45 deg raster gave the highest tensile strength; PETG intermediate between PLA and ABS. Specific MPa values UNVERIFIED.

title: Effects of part build orientations on fatigue behaviour of FDM-processed PLA material
key_fact_extracted: Fatigue of FDM PLA depends on build orientation (X, Y, 45 deg); 45 deg orientation gave the longest fatigue life. UNVERIFIED (abstract not retrieved).

title: On the fatigue strength of 3D-printed polylactide (PLA)
key_fact_extracted: Statistical re-analysis of published S-N data for 3D-printed PLA: provides a reference fatigue curve (negative inverse slope and endurance limit extrapolated at 2x10^6 cycles) for design at >95% survival probability; numeric limit not in abstract - UNVERIFIED.

title: Multi-Response Optimization of Tensile Creep Behavior of PLA 3D Printed Parts Using Categorical Response Surface Methodology
key_fact_extracted: Tensile creep of FDM PLA per ASTM D2990 (39 runs, CCD): creep minimised at 0.1 mm layer height and 100% infill (hexagonal pattern).

title: Numerical and experimental investigation on creep response of 3D printed Polylactic acid (PLA) samples. Part I: The effect of building direction and unidirectional raster orientation
journal: Journal of the Mechanical Behavior of Biomedical Materials
key_fact_extracted: Creep response of 3D-printed PLA depends on build direction and raster orientation; numerical model validated experimentally.

title: Thermal expansion coefficient determination of polylactic acid using digital image correlation
key_fact_extracted: Linear CTE of PLA printed discs (20% and 40% infill) measured by digital image correlation; numeric CTE value not in abstract - UNVERIFIED (typical literature range ~60-90 ppm/K).

title: Evaluation of dimensional accuracy and material properties of the MakerBot 3D desktop printer
key_fact_extracted: MakerBot Replicator 2: printed dimensions differed significantly (p<0.05) from nominal; layer height, infill and orientation affect properties - users must account for inherent dimensional limits.

title: Dimensional accuracy of FDM-printed polymer parts
key_fact_extracted: Dimensional accuracy of FDM-printed polymer parts (PLA, ABS): strip-width deviations vs nozzle diameter, temperature and speed. Specific +/- mm UNVERIFIED.

title: Surface Roughness Quality and Dimensional Accuracy—A Comprehensive Analysis of 100% Infill Printed Parts Fabricated by a Personal/Desktop Cost-Effective FDM 3D Printer
key_fact_extracted: Desktop FDM, 100% infill, 0.3 mm nozzle/0.1 mm layer: PLA+ most dimensionally accurate and smoothest of materials tested. Specific deviations UNVERIFIED.

title: Physical and mechanical properties of PLA, and their functions in widespread applications — A comprehensive review
key_fact_extracted: Comprehensive review of PLA physical/mechanical properties (bulk tensile modulus ~3-4 GPa, Tg ~55-60 C, brittle, hydrolytic degradation) - background for creep/thermal limits. Values from review, not re-verified here.

title: Design and experiment of generalized triple-cross-spring flexure pivots applied to the ultra-precision instruments
key_fact_extracted: Generalized triple-cross-spring flexure pivot: axis drift <0.3 um over +/-10 deg motion range (FEA, prototypes) - benchmark for achievable pivot accuracy.

key_fact_extracted: New list price US$22,689.99 (VWR, accessed Oct 2026). Section range 0.5-60 um.

key_fact_extracted: Listed at US$8,995 (GMI); refurbished HM325-2 US$7,950 (Rankin); used units US$1,215-2,150 (Bimedis, New Life Scientific).

key_fact_extracted: Refurbished RM2125 US$7,950 (1-yr warranty); used RM2125 RTS US$2,100-6,999 on secondary market.

title: Rocking microtome, Cambridge, England, 1885 (object 1885-50)
key_fact_extracted: Invented by Horace Darwin; razor fixed, specimen passes across it in an arc in a rocking motion; loaned to the museum as new technology in 1885; sold from 1885 and still available in the 20th century.

authors: Whipple Museum of the History of Science
title: Rocking microtome by Cambridge Scientific Instrument Company (accession 0683)
key_fact_extracted: Construction: cast-iron base, rocking arm on pivoting support; arm rests on threaded steel shaft with knurled screw; cog wheel at base moved by handled brass arm (ratchet feed); string-and-pulley drive; two springs from base to rocking arm.

title: Cambridge Scientific Instrument Company collection description
key_fact_extracted: Rocking microtome's simplicity allowed production at a fraction of the price of competitors and the design remained relatively unchanged until the 1970s.

title: Object 25: Cambridge rocker microtome
key_fact_extracted: Developed by Horace Darwin; first marketed 1885; described as one of the most successful microtomes ever invented.

title: Microtomy and Paraffin Section Preparation (citing 101 Steps to Better Histology)
key_fact_extracted: Disposable blades/knives have facet angle ~35 deg; Leica recommends a clearance angle of 1-5 deg; first sections of a ribbon from a cold block are thicker (thermal expansion); speed, clearance and edge condition affect actual thickness.

title: Troubleshooting in Microtomy
key_fact_extracted: Bevel + clearance + rake = 90 deg; disposable-blade clearance 5-10 deg (3-5 deg for hard tissue to prevent vibration, 7-10 deg for soft tissue to avoid compression); alternating thick-and-thin sections ('chatter') often resolved by clearance adjustment.
